newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan has 10-point program for U.N. reform.
newsitem.headline: Annan has 10-point program for U.N. reform.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, with an eye on the U.S. Congress, on Monday proposed eliminating staff and cutting $123 million from the budget as a first step towards reforming the world body.

Under pressure from the United States to begin reforms as soon as possible, Annan also proposed merging some U.N. departments, creating a code of conduct for u.N. employees and cutting administrative costs by a third by the year 2001.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Annan had called Secretary of State Madeleine Albright late on Sunday to alert her to the plan. U.N. sources said he had spoken to some U.S. Congressmen on Monday but they did not know the response.
"This is a serious proposal. It has been analysed. It has been discussed and we know that it will not gut the organisation," Annan said of his 10 proposals.

He said the U.N. budget of $1.3 billion a year would be reduced by $123 million in 1988-1999s and that 1,000 jobs his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, left vacant would now be cut completely.

Boutros-Ghali's proposal to cut the posts was rejected by the General Assembly. "But I am confident they will (approve) now because of the ground work and preparatory work we have done in moving it along," Annan said.

Ambassador Richard Butler of Australia, who has served on several U.N. reform groups, believed Annan, a Ghanaian, had served notice to the world body's Third World majority that he would increase funds for development but not jobs in New York.
"He is saying the job cuts are permanent. Forget it. This is not a gravy train," Butler said.

In addition to the permanent job cuts Annan said he would cut down administrative expenditures, now 38 percent of the budget. The estimated $200 million savings would be used for development projects.

And he said he would merge three departments dealing with economic and social programmes into one department, now headed by undersecretaries-general from China, India and France. Diplomats said they believed Nitin Desai of India would head the new department.

Annan also said he was revamping the Department of Public Information but no details on how this would be done were given. Butler said Annan had recognised that the "public relations here are appalling."

The announcements by Annan were the first part of a reform programme he promised to undertake when he assumed the job on Jan. 1 after the United States vetoed Boutros-Ghali for allegedly moving too slowly on reform. Payment of the more than $1 billion U.S. debt hinges on the pace of reform.
U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson immediately welcomed Annan's proposals, saying: "This is a big plus for reformers because it shows the secretary-general is out front on bold reforms."

"This announcement will help in our efforts to convince the Congress we should pay our arrears. It is the secretary-general who is out front as the top reformer," he said in an apparent reference to expected Congressional legislation setting conditions for reform.

Annan's initial proposals concerned the secretariat or core bureaucracy in New York, Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi of 9,000 people which he controls. Another estimated 40,000 people are employed by a network of specialised U.N. agencies, which have their own boards and fund-raising procedures. He expects to make proposals on their activities in June.

The conservative U.S. Congress has vowed not to pay the $1 billion Washington owes the world body until it was satisfied with Annan's reform programme. Many have doubts it will approve anywhere near the required level of debt.

Instead both the White House and Congress are insisting U.S. dues be cut further to 20 percent of the total, which means Europeans, who now pay 35 percent of the budget, and Japan would have to fill the gap.

But none of them is willing to lower U.S. dues unless there is a commitment to pay up. And Germany and Japan do not want to pay more unless they are given permanent seats on the 15-member Security Council.
